questions.prompt: A caller asks for a customer’s account balance. What should you do first?
options: Confirm identity using the bank’s approved checks
Share it if the caller knows the customer’s full name
Ask the caller to send an email request
Give only an approximate balance
questions.explanation: A name or other personal detail is not enough. Complete approved identity checks before sharing account information.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to send a statement to a new email address. What is the safest action?
options: Send it and ask them to confirm later
Follow the approved process to verify and update contact details
Send it to both the old and new addresses
Ask a nearby colleague whether the customer seems genuine
questions.explanation: A changed destination must be verified through the bank’s approved process before customer information is sent.

questions.prompt: A colleague from another department asks for a customer’s phone number but gives no reason. What should you do?
options: Share it because they work for the bank
Send it through personal chat
Check their work need and access permission first
Read it aloud so it is not written down
questions.explanation: Customer information should only be accessed and shared for an approved work purpose with authorised staff.

questions.prompt: You need to discuss a customer complaint at a busy counter. What is best?
options: Speak loudly so the queue can hear the explanation
Move the discussion to a suitable private place
Use the customer’s full name repeatedly
Ask the next customer to help translate the details
questions.explanation: Discuss personal or account details where other customers cannot overhear them.

questions.prompt: A printed account statement is left on the shared printer. What should you do?
options: Leave it in case the owner returns
Put it face down on the counter
Secure it promptly and follow the branch process to notify the owner or report exposure
Take a photo to identify the customer later
questions.explanation: Secure printed customer information promptly and report any possible exposure according to branch procedure.

questions.prompt: You see a customer’s account open on a screen while the employee steps away. What is the best response?
options: Lock the screen if you can do so safely and alert the employee
Read the account to see whether it is important
Leave it because the employee will return
Take a picture as proof
questions.explanation: Screens containing customer data should not be left visible to others. Do not inspect or copy information unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: Before sharing customer information with another employee, which checks should you make? Select ALL that apply.
options: They have an approved work reason
They are allowed to access that type of information
Only the information needed for the task is shared
They are friendly and work in the same building
questions.explanation: Use a valid work purpose, check authorisation, and share only what is needed. Familiarity alone is not permission.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to discuss an account with their relative. Which safeguards may be needed? Select ALL that apply.
options: Follow the bank’s process for checking the customer’s permission
Verify the relative’s identity where required
Share the full account history because they are family
Record the permission or action when the process requires it
questions.explanation: Family relationship alone does not give access. Follow the bank’s permission and identity process and record it as required.

questions.prompt: Match each customer-data situation to the safest response.
left: A caller asks for a balance
A statement is left at the printer
A colleague asks for extra customer details
right: Secure it and follow the exposure-reporting process
Check their work need and access permission
Complete the approved identity checks first
questions.explanation: Identity checks, authorised work access, and safe handling of documents help protect customer data.

questions.prompt: An email says your staff account will be closed in 10 minutes unless you sign in through a link. What should you do?
options: Use the link before the deadline
Reply with your staff ID
Do not use the link; report or verify through the bank’s known process
Forward it to the whole branch
questions.explanation: Urgency plus an unexpected sign-in link is a common warning sign. Use the approved reporting route.

questions.prompt: You receive an invoice attachment you were not expecting. What is best?
options: Open it to find out who sent it
Check with the sender through a known contact method before opening it
Save it to the shared drive for later
Send it to a customer to ask if they recognise it
questions.explanation: Unexpected attachments should be verified using a trusted route, not opened out of curiosity.

questions.prompt: The sender name says “Bank IT Helpdesk,” but the actual email address looks unfamiliar. What should you do?
options: Trust the sender name
Check the actual address and report it if unexpected
Reply asking whether it is real
Open any attachment to look for a logo
questions.explanation: Sender display names can be faked. Check the full email address and use approved reporting steps.

questions.prompt: An email appears in a familiar thread but asks you to use a new payment link. What is safest?
options: Trust it because the thread is familiar
Use it only if the logo looks correct
Verify the change through a known, independent contact route
Ask the sender to confirm by replying to the same email
questions.explanation: An attacker may take over or imitate a real email thread. Verify payment or link changes separately.

questions.prompt: A QR code on an unexpected notice says “Scan now to keep your staff access.” What should you do?
options: Scan it and sign in quickly
Avoid scanning it and verify the notice through an official channel
Share it with colleagues to see what it opens
Use your personal phone instead
questions.explanation: A QR code can hide a harmful website. Verify the request before opening it.

questions.prompt: You think an email may be a scam. What is the safest way to alert the bank?
options: Use the bank’s approved report-phishing method or service desk
Forward it to all staff with a warning
Reply to the sender and ask for proof
Delete it and tell nobody
questions.explanation: Use the bank’s approved reporting route. Broad forwarding may expose others to the same harmful content.

questions.prompt: A message asks you to sign in urgently. Which are warning signs? Select ALL that apply.
options: The link goes to an unfamiliar website
It asks you to keep the request secret
It threatens account closure unless you act immediately
It matches a task you were expecting and the link is verified
questions.explanation: Look for unexpected links, secrecy, pressure, and threats. A familiar task still needs normal checks when the message is unusual.

questions.prompt: Compare the two email notices. Select ALL meaningful warning signs in Message B.

b.title: URGENT: staff account at risk
b.request: Enter password and approve sign-in in 8 minutes
b.tone: Threatens lockout; says not to call IT

options: The sender address is different from the known address
The link uses an unfamiliar lookalike website
The message pressures the reader and asks for a password/MFA approval
Both messages ask staff to read a policy
questions.explanation: The sender, destination, urgent pressure, and request for secrets are meaningful warning signs. The details are fictional training examples.

questions.prompt: Compare the two supplier messages. Select ALL meaningful differences that need checking in Message B.

a.title: Invoice follow-up
a.request: Please confirm receipt of the invoice

b.title: Updated bank details — pay today
b.request: Change bank details now; do not call our usual number

options: The reply-to address does not match the normal address
The message requests a payment-detail change under pressure
The message says not to use the usual contact number
The invoice number is printed near the top
questions.explanation: Unexpected payment changes require independent verification, even when the email looks like an ongoing conversation.

questions.prompt: Match each email warning sign to the safest response.
left: New supplier bank details by email
right: Verify independently using a known contact
Do not open until the sender/request is verified
Do not sign in; report or check through an official channel
questions.explanation: Use trusted channels to check messages before clicking, opening files, or changing payment instructions.

questions.prompt: You realise a customer file was sent to the wrong external email address. What should you do first?
options: Try to hide the mistake until you know whether it was opened
Report it promptly through the bank’s incident process and follow instructions
Send another email asking the recipient to ignore it, then close the matter
Delete the sent email and do not mention it
questions.explanation: Report quickly. Do not conceal, delete records, or assume a follow-up message resolves the exposure.

questions.prompt: A workstation shows a strange warning and files appear to be changing names. What is the safest response?
options: Keep clicking to see what happens
Restart it several times
Stop using it and contact the approved IT/security support route immediately
Copy the files to a USB drive
questions.explanation: Avoid further interaction and do not attempt fixes or copy files. Follow the bank’s incident instructions so evidence is not disturbed.

questions.prompt: You lose a work phone that may contain bank email. What should you do?
options: Wait until the end of the week to see if it turns up
Report it immediately using the bank’s lost-device process
Ask a friend to track it using their account
Change random settings on any computer you can find
questions.explanation: A lost work device can expose information. Prompt reporting allows authorised teams to take the correct steps.

questions.prompt: A customer reports an unusual account transaction. What should you do?
options: Promise a refund before checking anything
Tell them to post the details on social media
Follow the bank’s fraud-reporting process and record the facts accurately
Ask for their PIN to check whether they made it
questions.explanation: Use the approved fraud process, record what the customer reports, and never ask for their PIN or password.

questions.prompt: A visitor gives you a USB drive labelled “urgent salary list.” What is best?
options: Plug it in on a spare computer
Ask another clerk to test it
Do not connect it; report it through the approved channel
Take it home and scan it later
questions.explanation: Unknown removable devices can carry harmful files. Do not connect them to bank equipment.

questions.prompt: Branching scenario: you notice a suspicious message and then learn a colleague may have clicked it. Choose what to do at each stage.

nodes.prompt: Stage 1 of 3 — The email asks for your password and says not to contact IT. What do you do?

options.text: Do not use the link; report it through the approved channel
Open the link to check whether it looks real
Forward it to other clerks to ask their opinion

nodes.prompt: Stage 2 of 3 — A colleague says they may have entered their password. What should happen next?

options.text: Tell them to report it immediately through the bank’s incident route
Wait to see whether their account stops working
Ask them to delete the email and keep quiet

nodes.prompt: Stage 2 of 3 — You opened the link while checking it. What is the safest next step now?

options.text: Stop interacting with it and contact the approved IT/security route
Enter a dummy password to test the page
Clear browser history so it cannot cause an issue

nodes.prompt: Stage 3 of 3 — What should the colleague do with the device and message while help arrives?

options.text: Follow support instructions and leave relevant messages/alerts intact
Delete everything related to the email
Install a cleaning tool from the internet

nodes.prompt: Stage 3 of 3 — You are asked to hide the incident until later. What should you do?

options.text: Report the facts promptly and do not delete records
Agree to wait unless money is lost
Delete the email to protect the team

nodes.prompt: Stage 3 of 3 — Support asks you to preserve the message and stop using the page. What should you do?

options.text: Follow the instructions and keep the original message available
Forward the link to your personal mailbox
Try the link on a second bank computer

nodes.prompt: Stage 3 of 3 — You are tempted to clear the browser and keep working. What is best?

options.text: Stop and report what happened; leave evidence intact
Clear the browser and say nothing
Ask a customer to check the page

questions.explanation: The safe path is to stop interacting, report quickly, be honest about any click or password entry, and preserve relevant messages and alerts. Do not delete files or try your own fixes.

questions.prompt: Put the response steps for a suspected security incident in the safest order.
options: Report promptly through the approved bank channel
Notice the suspicious activity or mistake
Follow instructions from the authorised response team
Avoid further actions that could change or erase evidence
questions.explanation: Notice the issue, report it promptly, avoid disturbing evidence, and follow the authorised response team’s instructions.

questions.prompt: A customer document was sent to the wrong person. Put these steps in order.
options: Record the facts accurately using the bank’s process
Report the mistake promptly
Follow instructions on contacting the recipient or limiting exposure
Notice that the message went to the wrong address
questions.explanation: The event should be reported and documented, and any next steps should follow the bank’s process rather than improvised contact.

questions.prompt: Mini tabletop: a staff member reports a possible ransomware warning on their branch computer. Select ALL appropriate first actions.
options: Tell the approved IT/security contact promptly
Stop using the affected computer and follow support instructions
Take a phone photo of customer data on screen and send it to friends
Do not delete the warning or try random repair steps
Plug in a USB drive to copy documents before they change
questions.explanation: Prompt reporting, stopping further use, and preserving the warning help the authorised team respond. Avoid copying data or attempting fixes.

questions.prompt: After a possible data or device incident, which actions help avoid damaging evidence? Select ALL that apply.
options: Keep relevant emails, alerts, and records available
Report what happened honestly, including mistakes
Follow the instructions given by the authorised support team
Delete messages that look embarrassing
Try several repair tools before reporting
questions.explanation: Keep the relevant records and report honestly. Do not delete, alter, or try to repair evidence before authorised guidance.

questions.prompt: A customer’s ID details do not match the bank record. What should you do?
options: Override the mismatch because the customer is known
Follow the bank’s verification process and escalate if it remains unresolved
Use the details provided by the person waiting with them
Complete the transaction and fix the record later
questions.explanation: Do not bypass verification. Use the approved process and escalate unresolved differences.

questions.prompt: A customer’s relative asks for account details and says the customer is unable to come to the branch. What is best?
options: Share the details because they are family
Ask the relative to show any photo ID, then share everything
Follow the bank’s rules for permission and authority before sharing details
Read out only the balance
questions.explanation: Family connection does not automatically authorise access to a customer account.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to write their PIN down so they do not forget it. What should you do?
options: Write it on a slip and hand it over
Explain that secret credentials must not be written or shared by staff; guide them to approved help
Store it in a branch drawer
Tell another clerk the PIN so they can remind the customer
questions.explanation: Staff must never collect or store customer PINs/passwords. Use approved support guidance.

questions.prompt: A manager asks you in a chat to skip a required check because the queue is long. What should you do?
options: Skip it because the manager asked
Complete the required check and raise the concern through the proper route
Ask the waiting customers to vote
Mark the check complete without doing it
questions.explanation: Pressure or a senior request does not make an unapproved shortcut acceptable. Do the required check and escalate.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to change their contact details but cannot complete the usual checks. What should you do?
options: Change it because they are physically present
Use another employee’s login to process it
Explain that the required checks must be completed and follow the exception process
Write the new number on a sticky note for later
questions.explanation: Use the approved identity and exception process. Do not use another employee’s access or informal notes as a substitute.

questions.prompt: You notice a required compliance field is blank before completing a transaction. What should you do?
options: Complete it using a guess
Leave it blank and continue
Complete or resolve it accurately before proceeding, following procedure
Copy the value from an unrelated customer
questions.explanation: Records must be accurate and complete. Never guess or copy details from unrelated records.

questions.prompt: A customer complains that a transaction was not authorised. What is the best way to record it?
options: Write only what you personally believe happened
Use clear factual notes, the customer’s words where useful, and the required reporting process
Promise the complaint will be removed from their record
Change the date so it appears more recent
questions.explanation: Record facts clearly and honestly. Do not make promises or alter records to make the case look better.

questions.prompt: Which actions support compliance and fair customer handling? Select ALL that apply.
options: Complete the required identity checks
Record transactions and complaints accurately
Escalate a request that appears to bypass a required control
Skip checks for customers you know well
questions.explanation: Compliance applies consistently. Familiarity and workload do not replace required checks or accurate records.

questions.prompt: Match each compliance situation to the right action.
right: Follow permission and authority rules before disclosure
Resolve the missing information accurately before proceeding
Use the approved verification process and escalate if unresolved
questions.explanation: Use the approved procedures for identity, records, and authority to access information.

questions.prompt: A caller says they are from IT and asks you to read out the code sent to your phone. What should you do?
options: Read it if they know your employee number
Refuse to share the code and verify/report the request through an official channel
Send a screenshot of the code
Ask them to call back after lunch and then share it
questions.explanation: One-time codes and approval prompts are secrets. Do not share them with callers, even if they claim to be IT.

questions.prompt: Someone claiming to be a senior manager messages you to send customer records to a personal email urgently. What is best?
options: Send them because the request is urgent
Verify the request using a known official contact route and follow data-sharing rules
Send a small sample first
Ask another clerk to forward the records instead
questions.explanation: Use a trusted, independent channel to verify unusual requests and follow customer-data rules.

questions.prompt: A person carrying boxes asks you to hold a restricted door because they have no access card. What should you do?
options: Hold the door because their hands are full
Let them follow another employee inside
Direct them to the visitor/access process and do not allow unauthorised entry
Give them your access card for a minute
questions.explanation: Do not let someone bypass access controls because they sound reasonable or appear busy.

questions.prompt: A caller asks for the names and shift times of staff who handle cash. What should you do?
options: Provide the schedule if they sound polite
Share only the first names
Do not disclose staff/security details; verify the request through the official channel
Ask them to call another branch for it
questions.explanation: Staffing and security information should not be disclosed without an approved work need.

questions.prompt: A delivery worker asks to use your computer to print a label. What is safest?
options: Log in and let them use it while you watch
Give them your login for one minute
Decline and follow the branch’s visitor and printing process
Open your email and let them print directly
questions.explanation: Visitors should not use your logged-in workstation or account. Follow the approved visitor and printing process.

questions.prompt: A caller becomes angry and insists you must bypass checks to prevent a complaint. What is best?
options: Bypass the check to calm them down
Stay polite, follow the required process, and escalate the complaint if needed
End the call without recording it
Ask them to send their password to prove who they are
questions.explanation: Keep a professional tone while following required checks and escalation routes.

questions.prompt: Branching scenario: a caller claims to be the fraud team and says an account will be locked unless you help immediately.

nodes.prompt: Stage 1 of 3 — The caller asks you to read an employee sign-in code. What do you do?

options.text: Do not share it; end or pause the call and verify through a known official number
Share it because they know the branch name
Read only the first half of the code

nodes.prompt: Stage 2 of 3 — You call the known official number, but cannot confirm the caller’s request. What next?

options.text: Report the suspicious call and follow the bank’s process
Call the unknown number back to ask again
Wait until the end of the shift before telling anyone

nodes.prompt: Stage 2 of 3 — You already shared some information. What is best now?

options.text: Report exactly what you shared, promptly, through the approved route
Delete the call log to avoid trouble
Keep quiet unless you see a loss

nodes.prompt: Stage 3 of 3 — What should you record about the call?

options.text: The time, number, claimed role, request, and action taken, following policy
Only your opinion about the caller
Nothing, because no code was shared

nodes.prompt: Stage 3 of 3 — A colleague suggests approving the request to avoid delay. What should you do?

options.text: Do not approve an unverified request; report it and follow procedure
Approve it if the caller sounds confident
Use a customer account to test it

nodes.prompt: Stage 3 of 3 — You have reported the disclosure. What should you do next?

options.text: Follow the authorised response instructions and keep relevant records
Try to fix the account yourself without telling anyone else
Delete the messages and continue as normal

nodes.prompt: Stage 3 of 3 — You are worried you may be blamed. What is the right choice?

options.text: Report the facts honestly and promptly
Hide the activity unless someone asks
Ask the caller what you should write in the report

questions.explanation: Never share codes, passwords, or approvals with a caller. Verify using a known official route, report suspicious requests, and be honest if any information was disclosed.

questions.prompt: Which are common signs of social engineering? Select ALL that apply.
options: A caller pressures you to act immediately
A person asks you to keep a request secret from your manager
A request asks you to bypass normal checks
A caller is happy for you to verify through the official number
questions.explanation: Pressure, secrecy, and requests to bypass checks are warning signs. Legitimate requests should allow normal verification.

questions.prompt: A customer says they gave their OTP to someone who called them. What should you do?
options: Tell them nothing can be done
Follow the bank’s fraud-reporting process promptly and guide them to the official channel
Ask them to tell you the OTP so you can check it
Tell them to wait for another call
questions.explanation: Treat potential credential disclosure urgently. Do not ask them to repeat the OTP; follow the bank’s incident/fraud process.

questions.prompt: A customer reports a debit they do not recognise. What should you say first?
options: “You must have forgotten making it.”
“Please post the transaction on social media.”
“I will help record the details and follow our official fraud-reporting process.”
“Give me your PIN so I can check.”
questions.explanation: Listen, record relevant facts, and use the official process. Never ask for the customer’s secret credentials.

questions.prompt: A customer says a caller told them to install a screen-sharing app to receive a refund. What is safest?
options: Help install the app to finish the refund quickly
Explain the risk and guide them to the bank’s official support/fraud route
Ask the customer to share their screen with you through your personal account
Tell them to call the same number back
questions.explanation: Unexpected remote-access requests are a common scam pattern. Use official support and fraud reporting routes.

questions.prompt: A customer says their phone suddenly lost service and then they received account alerts they did not expect. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a possible fraud warning and follow the bank’s escalation process
Tell them to buy a new phone first
Ask them to share their password with you
Ignore it unless they see a cash loss
questions.explanation: Sudden loss of service alongside unexpected account alerts can indicate a risk. Record the facts and escalate promptly.

questions.prompt: A customer shows you a message promising a guaranteed investment return and asking for a bank transfer today. What is best?
options: Encourage the transfer if the return is high
Use the message link to check the investment
Warn against rushing, avoid endorsing it, and follow the bank’s reporting/advice process
Ask for their online banking password so you can help
questions.explanation: Do not endorse high-pressure promises or use their link. Guide the customer to approved channels and report suspicious activity.

questions.prompt: A customer says they approved an unexpected sign-in prompt. What should you do?
options: Tell them to ignore it
Follow the bank’s account-security/fraud process and record what they report
Ask them to approve another prompt to test it
Tell them to delete all alerts
questions.explanation: Unexpected approvals should be treated as a potential compromise and escalated promptly.

questions.prompt: A customer reports possible online banking fraud. Put the actions in the best order.
options: Record the key facts accurately using the bank’s process
Listen calmly and identify the concern
Follow the official fraud escalation and customer guidance process
Do not ask for or record passwords, PINs, or OTPs
questions.explanation: Listen, avoid collecting secrets, document the relevant facts, then follow the official fraud process.

questions.prompt: A customer reports a possible scam. Which details are useful to record under the bank’s process? Select ALL that apply.
options: Approximate time and what happened
Contact number or message details, where permitted by policy
What action the customer says they took
The customer’s full password or OTP
questions.explanation: Record relevant facts and preserve relevant messages as directed, but never ask for or record secrets such as passwords, PINs, or OTPs.

questions.prompt: Mini tabletop: a customer says they followed a caller’s instructions, installed a remote-access app, and then saw a debit alert. Select ALL suitable actions for a front-desk employee.
options: Stay calm, record the customer’s report, and escalate through the official fraud route
Tell the customer to contact the bank using a verified official channel
Ask for their banking password to confirm the transaction
Tell them to delete the app and all messages before reporting
Follow the bank’s process for urgent fraud concerns and instructions
questions.explanation: Front-line staff should collect relevant facts, avoid secrets or improvised technical support, and promptly use the official fraud route.

questions.prompt: In an email, the visible sender name says “Customer Support,” but the address is helpdesk@bank-account-check.example. What does that suggest?
options: The display name proves it is genuine
The address is worth checking because the sender name can be faked
All email addresses ending in .example are safe
It is safe if the email has a logo
questions.explanation: The full sender address matters; a display name and logo can be copied.

questions.prompt: An email’s “Reply-To” address differs from the “From” address. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a warning sign and verify the request before replying or acting
Ignore the difference every time
Send a test password to check it
Assume the email is genuine if it arrived in a known thread
questions.explanation: A different reply-to address may be legitimate, but it needs checking when unexpected or linked to sensitive requests.

questions.prompt: A mail security result says an email authentication check failed. What should you conclude?
options: It definitely came from the bank
Ignore it if the message is well written
Treat it cautiously and use the bank’s reporting/verification process
Forward it to the customer for confirmation
questions.explanation: Failed authentication is a warning, not the only factor in a decision. Do not act on the message without verification.

questions.prompt: Why can the “Received” lines in an email header be useful?
options: They may help trained support staff review the route the email took
They show whether a customer has enough money
They guarantee that a sender is honest
They can safely be ignored in every investigation
questions.explanation: Headers can help authorised staff investigate message routing, but they are not proof by themselves.

questions.prompt: You are unsure how to view the full email header. What is the safest choice?
options: Use an unknown online header checker with the whole email
Copy the email to your personal mailbox
Use the bank-approved mail option or ask the service desk for help
Delete the original and keep a screenshot only
questions.explanation: Use approved tools and support routes. Do not upload bank emails or customer data to unapproved websites.

questions.prompt: A forwarded email has no clear original sender details. What should you do before acting on a payment request?
options: Trust the colleague who forwarded it
Ask them to send the original details and verify independently through the known contact route
Click the link to find the original sender
Use the reply button to ask for bank details
questions.explanation: Forwarding can hide or remove context. Verify sensitive requests using original details and a trusted channel.

questions.prompt: Compare the two header summaries. Select ALL items that make Message B more suspicious.
options: The sender domain is not the known bank domain
The reply-to points to a different unfamiliar address
The authentication result is shown as failed
The message subject says “statement”
questions.explanation: Sender and reply-to differences plus failed authentication and pressure deserve verification. Header fields alone should be reviewed in context.

questions.prompt: Two messages ask a clerk to review a customer complaint. Select ALL differences that should trigger extra checks in Message B.

a.request: Review the case in the normal work system

b.request: Enter staff password and send a screenshot of the customer record
b.tone: Do this secretly before your manager returns

options: Different, lookalike sender domain
Unfamiliar sign-in destination
Request to send customer data and keep it secret
Both messages refer to a complaint
questions.explanation: The unfamiliar sender/link, request for customer data, and secrecy are meaningful warning signs.

questions.prompt: Match each email detail to what it can tell you.
right: May help authorised staff review the route a message took
Shows the address claiming to have sent the message
questions.explanation: Email details can provide clues but need to be reviewed carefully and through approved tools.

questions.prompt: Before acting on an unusual email, which checks can help? Select ALL that apply.
options: Read the full sender address
Check the reply-to and link destination when relevant
Use the approved reporting or verification route
Assume a logo and correct spelling make it safe
questions.explanation: Look at the actual address and destination, then verify or report unusual requests. Appearance alone is not proof.

questions.prompt: A supplier emails new bank details and asks that today’s payment be made immediately. What should you do?
options: Change the details based only on the email
Verify the change through the bank’s approved independent process before any update
Reply to the same email asking “Are you sure?”
Ask a colleague to use their login to make the payment
questions.explanation: Payment changes must be independently verified using approved contacts and controls, not only the message that requested the change.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to send their account record to a personal email address. What is safest?
options: Send it if they ask politely
Use a personal email but remove the account number
Follow the bank’s approved document delivery and address-verification process
Ask the customer to sign a blank form first
questions.explanation: Personal email or an unverified destination may not be approved for customer records. Follow the formal process.

questions.prompt: You see a mismatch between an invoice amount and the payment record. What should you do?
options: Change one amount so it matches
Ask the supplier by replying to the same email
Pause the processing step and resolve the mismatch through the approved process
Pay it and make a note later
questions.explanation: Do not guess or quietly alter records. Resolve the mismatch and follow the approved payment process.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to backdate an entry so a missed deadline looks on time. What should you do?
options: Backdate it if the amount is correct
Make the entry accurate and raise the request through the proper route
Use the date from a similar transaction
Delete the record and start again without telling anyone
questions.explanation: Records must show what actually happened. Never falsify dates or conceal mistakes.

questions.prompt: A payment request arrives through an unofficial messaging app. What is the best next step?
options: Process it because the person’s name is familiar
Ask them to send a voice note
Move the request into the bank’s approved workflow and verify it before action
Save the message as proof and pay it
questions.explanation: Use approved channels, verification, and workflow for payment instructions.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to correct a transaction note. What should you do?
options: Change it to what they prefer without checking
Follow the approved correction process and keep an accurate record of the change
Delete the old record
Ask the next shift to handle it without a note
questions.explanation: Corrections should be authorised, traceable, and accurate.

questions.prompt: A payment instruction has all required fields but comes from a new email address. What should you do?
options: Proceed because the form is complete
Check the sender and instruction using the required independent verification process
Ask the sender to confirm by replying to the same message
Process it if the amount is small
questions.explanation: Complete fields do not prove that a request is genuine. Follow the established verification checks.

questions.prompt: Put the steps for a supplier bank-detail change in the safest order.
options: Record the approved change in the official system
Receive an unexpected change request
Verify it independently using a known contact route
Obtain the required approval before making the change
questions.explanation: Receive the request, verify independently, obtain required approval, then update the official record.

questions.prompt: Which actions help keep payment records safe and accurate? Select ALL that apply.
options: Use the approved payment workflow
Verify bank-detail changes independently
Keep a clear record of required approvals
Backdate entries when work is delayed
questions.explanation: Approved workflow, independent checks, and traceable approval protect payment records. Do not change history to hide delays.

questions.prompt: Someone you do not recognise walks behind you through a staff-only door. What should you do?
options: Assume a customer service employee invited them
Follow branch access/visitor procedure and alert the appropriate staff or security contact
Give them your access card
Ignore it if they carry a laptop
questions.explanation: Restricted areas require authorised access. Do not lend credentials or assume someone else checked.

questions.prompt: A document containing customer details is left on the counter after closing. What should you do?
options: Leave it for the morning shift
Place it in a secure approved location and report the exposure if required
Take it home so nobody sees it
Put it in ordinary rubbish
questions.explanation: Secure customer paperwork according to the branch process and report possible exposure as required.

questions.prompt: A visitor asks to borrow your staff badge because they forgot theirs. What is best?
options: Lend it if they return it quickly
Walk them through the staff entrance
Refuse and direct them to the approved visitor/access process
Let them use your badge only in the lobby
questions.explanation: Never lend staff badges or access credentials.

questions.prompt: A customer starts reading their account number aloud in a crowded queue. What should you do?
options: Repeat it loudly to confirm
Help move the discussion to a more private place
Write it on a public board
Ask the queue to move closer
questions.explanation: Protect customer privacy by moving sensitive discussion away from others where possible.

questions.prompt: You find a pile of old printouts with customer names beside the printer. What should you do?
options: Put them in an open tray for the owner
Use the approved secure disposal method or ask the responsible person to handle it
Take them to the break room
Photograph the list before disposing of it
questions.explanation: Customer information must be disposed of using approved secure methods, not ordinary open waste.

questions.prompt: A stranger says they are here to repair a terminal but has no visible authorisation. What should you do?
options: Let them start because they sound confident
Ask them for your password first
Follow the visitor/vendor check-in process and confirm authorisation before access
Give them a customer-free workstation
questions.explanation: Vendor work requires the correct authorisation and check-in process before access is provided.

questions.prompt: During an evacuation alarm, what should take priority?
options: Saving paperwork from the desk
Following the branch emergency procedure and moving to safety
Completing the customer queue first
Returning to lock every drawer even if unsafe
questions.explanation: Follow the branch emergency plan and prioritise people’s safety. Do not delay evacuation to protect records.

questions.prompt: You notice a public noticeboard has a sheet with staff phone numbers and shift details. What should you do?
options: Leave it because staff information is not customer data
Take it down if authorised and report it through the appropriate branch process
Post a photo in the staff group
Add more details so it is clearer
questions.explanation: Staffing and contact information can create security risks. Follow the branch process to secure and report it.

questions.prompt: Which actions help keep a branch secure? Select ALL that apply.
options: Challenge or report unauthorised access using branch procedure
Keep customer papers and screens away from public view
Use the approved visitor/vendor check-in process
Lend your badge to someone who forgot theirs
questions.explanation: Access controls, privacy and visitor checks help protect the branch. Do not lend badges.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for an unknown visitor requesting access to a staff-only area in order.
options: Confirm their visit/authorisation through the approved process
Do not let them enter using your badge
Direct them to the authorised reception or visitor procedure
Notify the appropriate branch/security contact if the request remains suspicious
questions.explanation: Do not allow unauthorised entry; direct the visitor to the correct process, verify permission, and escalate any concern.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks to use your login because theirs is not working. What should you do?
options: Share it for one task
Type the password for them and let them continue under your name
Do not share it; direct them to the approved access-help process
Create a simple shared password for the team
questions.explanation: Each person must use their own approved account. Shared logins make actions hard to trace.

questions.prompt: You receive an MFA approval prompt but are not trying to sign in. What should you do?
options: Approve it to clear the alert
Deny or ignore it as appropriate and report it through the bank’s approved process
Send a screenshot of the prompt to a friend
Keep approving until it stops
questions.explanation: Unexpected sign-in prompts may indicate someone has your password. Do not approve them; report promptly.

questions.prompt: You need to leave your desk briefly while the customer system is open. What should you do?
options: Lock the screen before stepping away
Minimise the window only
Ask a customer to watch the screen
Leave it open because you will be quick
questions.explanation: Lock the screen when you leave, even briefly.

questions.prompt: A pop-up says you must install a new “security tool” from an unfamiliar website to continue work. What is best?
options: Install it if the pop-up uses the bank logo
Ask a colleague to download it instead
Do not install it; check with the approved IT/service desk route
Use your personal laptop to install and transfer it
questions.explanation: Only use software and installation processes approved by the bank.

questions.prompt: You find an unknown USB device beside the teller counter. What should you do?
options: Plug it in to identify the owner
Take it to an approved contact without connecting it to any device
Use it only on a spare workstation
Give it to a customer who asks about it
questions.explanation: Do not connect unknown devices to bank systems. Follow the branch process for handling found property.

questions.prompt: A password reset email arrives that you did not request. What should you do?
options: Use the link to see which account it affects
Ignore it and approve any follow-up prompts
Do not use unexpected links; report or verify through the approved channel
Forward it to your personal email for later
questions.explanation: Unrequested reset emails can indicate someone is trying to access the account. Use approved verification/reporting.

questions.prompt: You need to access bank systems while travelling. Which option is safest?
options: Use any public computer available
Use only the bank-approved device and access method
Ask a hotel worker to log in for you
Use a stranger’s Wi-Fi and save your password
questions.explanation: Use only approved devices, connections and access methods for bank work.

questions.prompt: A colleague has written their password on a sticky note near the monitor. What should you do?
options: Copy it in case they forget
Leave it visible because it is their account
Alert the colleague and follow the bank’s process to correct the unsafe practice
Use it only if they are on leave
questions.explanation: Passwords should not be left visible. Help correct the practice and report repeated or serious issues according to policy.

questions.prompt: Which are safe account and device habits? Select ALL that apply.
options: Use your own account and do not share passwords
Lock the screen when leaving the desk
Report unexpected sign-in or password-reset prompts
Approve an MFA prompt you did not start
questions.explanation: Use individual accounts, lock the screen, and report unexpected prompts. Never approve a sign-in you did not initiate.
